title: Richard Hooker
hook: an Anglican theologian of patient reason and tradition

segments.voice: Yesterday, Calvin and providence. Your line was held in his hand. Which uncertain thing did you set down, even for a breath? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-eight.

One London church, two preachers who disagreed. The story is often told that one of them preached in the morning and the other answered him from the same pulpit in the afternoon, Sunday after Sunday. The congregation got a debate with their sermons. One of those preachers was Richard Hooker. Years later, away from London, he wrote a long, careful book on the questions behind that quarrel, Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity. Today: an Anglican theologian who argued without contempt.

Hooker's opponents held that the church's order and worship should be drawn from scripture, chapter and verse. Hooker gave scripture first place too. But he asked a quiet question: is scripture the only light God gives? His answer was no. God is a God of order, Hooker said, and gave human beings reason, the power to see what is good and fitting, as a gift. Where scripture speaks plainly, it rules. Where it's silent, Christians use reason, and they listen to what the church has learned over the centuries, its tradition. Later teachers summed this up in a picture, a three-legged stool: scripture, reason, tradition. The stool isn't in Hooker's book, and he gave scripture more weight than an even stool suggests. But the picture catches one thing he cared about: no single support has to carry everything alone. For Hooker, reason wasn't faith's enemy. Scripture invites it. In Isaiah the LORD says, "Come now, and let us reason together." And First Peter asks Christians to be ready "to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear." With meekness. Hooker's style matched those words. He wrote about the people he disagreed with without sneering, and tried to state their case fairly before he answered it. Anglican churches look back to him as one of their shaping voices. Other Christians weigh scripture, reason and tradition differently, and argue about how. Hooker's way suggests the argument itself can be held with patience.

Here's the practice: be patient in argument. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you disagree with, about church, politics, family plans, anything. Now try Hooker's habit. In your head, state their view as fairly as you can, the way they'd put it on a good day, until they might nod along. Notice the urge to slip in a jab. Leave it out. Only then, if you like, shape your own answer, slowly and kindly. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name. The bell holds the time.
Richard Hooker. The Anglican theologian of patient reason: scripture first, with reason and tradition as gifts beside it.
Your line: reason is a gift. Today, in one disagreement, listen until you can say the other side's view back to them before you give yours. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Anglican and Episcopal Christians look to Richard Hooker when they speak of scripture, reason and tradition together; churches across traditions weigh these three in different ways in their teaching and decisions.

fork.reveal: in time, Hooker's fullest answer was the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity: long, patient, and courteous to the people he argued with.
